1:
Ellicott sets out what kind of chapter this is. Its precepts reach the Israelite's whole life, towards God and towards man. The authorities of the second Temple called it an embodying of the Decalogue, and read it in public as holding the sum and substance of the Law. He counts sixteen groups of precepts, eight closing with I am the Lord your God and eight with the shorter I am the Lord, and it is that formula which links the whole together. He marks the address too. Moses is told to speak to all the congregation of Israel, a phrase found nowhere else in Leviticus and only once more in the Pentateuch, at the institution of the Passover. Henry draws the same conclusion. The summary went not to Aaron and his sons only but to all the people, since all were concerned to know their duty; and even in the darker ages of the law, that religion could not be of God which boasted of ignorance as its mother.

Calvin takes the opening command as the key to everything after it. Men are not to measure the service of God by their own conceits but by his nature, and must begin by purifying themselves. Nothing is harder, since men lie slumbering in their own filthiness and seek to cloak it under the outward appearance of religion. So they are recalled to the imitation of God, who in adopting them meant that they should bear his image, as undegenerate children resemble their father. Though the most perfect fall far short even of the angels, the weakness of the humblest does not forbid him to aspire after that example. Keil and Delitzsch call the same command both the principle on which all that follows rests and the goal Israel was to keep in view.

Reverence for parents and the keeping of the sabbaths come first, and Keil and Delitzsch call them the two leading pillars of moral government and social well-being. The order of the parents is noticed by everyone. Ellicott says this is one of only three places in Scripture where the mother is named first, and reports the second-Temple explanation: children commonly fear the father and love the mother, so she is put first to teach that both are to be feared alike. Wesley gives another reason, that the duty is commonly neglected towards her, since children do not depend on her as on their father.

Why the sabbath should be joined to that commandment then divides them. Ellicott and Wesley read the pairing as a limit set on obedience: if parents should command the profanation of the day, the children must not obey them. Henry reads it the other way, as a charge to parents to use their authority for the honour of God's sabbaths, and observes that the ruin of young people has often begun in contempt of parents and profanation of the day. On the idols there is no division at all. Clarke translates elilim literally as nothings, the very thing the apostle meant in saying an idol is nothing in the world, and Ellicott gets the same force from the verb, since turn not is face not and forbids even examining one. Henry puts it as absurdity: men who are the work of God's hands worshipping gods that are the work of their own. Ellicott explains why the peace offering follows, Israel having sacrificed to idols the beasts meant for their own table. Keil and Delitzsch add that fidelity showed itself in keeping the sacrificial flesh holy, none eaten on the third day, on pain of extermination; and Gill, Wesley and Ellicott agree the offering in view must be the vow or the freewill kind, since the thanksgiving sort had to be eaten the same day.
9:
Ellicott makes the gleaning laws part of the holiness the chapter is after. As the Lord provides for every living creature, so must the Israelite regard the needy; and by fixing the right in law it releases the poor from private charity, which might have been capricious and tyrannical. He reports how the second Temple worked it out. The corner had no fixed measure, but never less than a sixtieth of the field, and it was left at the far end where the poor could get at it. They came three times, morning, noon and the evening sacrifice: the morning for mothers whose young children were still asleep, midday for the nurses, evening for the old. Keil and Delitzsch add the olive-yard, where the shaking of the boughs to reach what the sticks had missed was expressly forbidden, so that something remained for the stranger and the orphan and the widow.

The command against stealing then follows, and Ellicott ties it back to what precedes. Its first reference is to the owners of fields and vineyards, who commit theft by depriving the poor of what the law has assigned them; hence the canonists ruled that a man who sets a basket under his vine at the vintage robs the poor. Gill adds Aben Ezra's word that he who sees a theft and keeps silent is himself as the thief. Calvin reads the whole group as one prohibition worked out in its parts, since God enumerates as thefts the cases where either deceit or violence is used, the two words standing as genus and species, the second being open rapine. Henry keeps it plain: whatever we have in the world we must see that it be honestly come by, for we cannot be truly rich, nor long rich, with what is not.

False swearing is treated as the end of a chain rather than a separate crime. Gill passes on the rabbinic sequence, that stealing leads to dealing falsely, and that to lying, and lying to the oath; Wesley says the same. Gill adds that the prohibition covers not the proper name only but every name of God, so that a man who swears by him that made the heavens is caught by it. The wages of the hireling belong to the same group, and Calvin presses hardest here. Hirelings live from hand to mouth, so that the least delay leaves them without food, and a rich man who keeps such a one in suspense deprives him as it were of life. Henry calls the deferring of wages a sin that cries to heaven for vengeance, and Ellicott quotes the second-Temple judgment that he who treats a hireling harshly sins as if he had taken away life.

The deaf and the blind close the group. Calvin sets them under the sixth commandment, which covers every wrong by which men are unjustly injured. If any particle of humanity is in us we shall be anxious lest a blind man stumble, and shall spare the deaf, since to insult them is no less absurd than to assail stones with reproaches. Clarke says that a man capable of the stumbling-block must have a heart cased with cruelty. Whether that block is a real one is disputed. Ellicott and Henry both report the reading that obtained in the time of Christ, which took the words figuratively of imposing on the ignorant and misdirecting those who ask advice, Henry noting that the Jewish writers thought no one could be barbarous enough for the literal sense. Ellicott extends the deaf man to anyone out of hearing, and gives the reason for the closing clause. Deafness and blindness may keep the sufferer from ever bringing his man to an earthly court; but God hears when the human ear is stopped, and sees when the human eye is extinct.
15:
Ellicott reads the judgment law as a correction of the verse before it. The consideration just commanded for the infirm must not follow the poor man into court. The judge is to give sentence even if the poor party is thereby reduced to greater poverty, and even where the rich party would benevolently rather lose. He quotes the second-Temple illustration: if the rich man says, I am bound by law to provide for the poor, so I will let him win the suit and he will be supplied without the humiliation of alms — for that reason it is written, thou shalt not respect the person of the poor. Keil and Delitzsch put the same thing in two verbs. To respect the person of the poor is to act partially out of unmanly pity; to adorn the person of the great is to favour him in the decision. Wesley says only that pity must not produce an unrighteous sentence, and Gill divides the charge between the judge who pronounces and the witness who testifies, since justice may be perverted from either side. Ellicott adds how far the impartiality was carried, some holding that while a rich man and a poor man were tried both should be dressed alike, both stand or sit alike, and both be addressed by the judge in the same courteous manner.

The talebearer is identified by his trade. Gill says the word means a merchant, and particularly a pedlar in drugs and spices who goes from place to place, and so came to mean one who carries stories from house to house. Clarke does not restrain himself: such a man gets the secrets of every person and family and retails them wherever he goes, than which a more despicable character does not exist, and he should be exiled from the habitations of men. Calvin reports two derivations. Some take it from the merchant, since the whisperer is no less busy hunting for false reports to circulate than the trader is bent on buying and selling; others suppose a letter changed, so that the word comes from the foot, calumniators being always on the move to find grounds of detraction, which is why a verb of walking is always joined to it. His own account is of vagabonds who in their malignant inquisitiveness penetrate everybody's secrets to bring quiet people into trouble. Ellicott gives the verdict of the second Temple, that idolatry, incest and murder remove a man from this world and the next, but slander surpasses them all, since it kills three with one act, the man who speaks, the man spoken of, and the man who listens.

What it means to stand against a neighbour's blood is disputed. Ellicott takes the clause literally and finds in it a duty of rescue: a man who sees another drowning or set upon by robbers or wild beasts must not stand by while the blood is shed, but is to help at the hazard of his own life. The same reading covers the courtroom, so that one who knows a man has shed blood must not stand silently by while the cause is tried; and he cites the Chaldee, thou shalt not keep silent the blood of thy neighbour when thou knowest the truth. Others, he notes, take it the opposite way, of coming forward to procure a false sentence of blood. Wesley and Clarke both read it of the false witness, Wesley observing that accusers and witnesses stand while the judges sit, and Clarke that by such testimony the life of an innocent man is endangered. Gill reaches the duty of rescue from the verse that follows: a man who does not try to save his neighbour, whether by testimony or by delivering him from drowning or from beasts and thieves, is by interpretation hating him.
17:
Calvin insists the clause be taken by itself, and makes it the proof that the sixth commandment reaches inward. Murder was forbidden not only by the hand or the weapon but in the cherishing of hatred and ill-will. This confirms Paul's word that the law is spiritual, and refutes the folly of those who pretend Moses was an earthly lawgiver to the Jews like Lycurgus or Solon, since he penetrates even to the secret affections. Calvin thinks John drew his saying that a hater of his brother is a murderer from this verse, since though no outward sign appear, the inward feeling is accounted murder before God. Gill gives the two ways the hatred shows itself: not saving a neighbour's life when it could be saved, and not reproving him but suffering him to go on to his ruin. Wesley makes the second the sharper of the two. A man who will neither divulge his brother's wrong nor tell him of it, but smothers his hatred in sullen silence, is hating him in the very act of keeping quiet.

The rebuke commanded next is hedged about carefully. Calvin sees the danger in it plainly: many under the pretext of conscientiousness are rigid censors of others and burst out in the open proclamation of their defects, objecting that sin is nourished by silence unless everyone is eager to reprove it. He answers that the remedy is to bring the wanderer back by private rebuke and not by publishing his offence, for whoever triumphs in his brother's infamy precipitates his ruin. An immoderate love of fault-finding, he concludes, will always be found arrogant and cruel. Clarke gives the practical form of the same rule: speak to him privately if you can, and if you cannot, write to him in such a way that he alone shall see it. Ellicott adds the limit the second Temple set: the reproof must be repeated if it fails, but the rebuker must stop the moment he sees blushes on the offender's face, since every further step is an unnecessary humiliation and brings the sin back on the man who reproves. Keil and Delitzsch settle the grammar the same way: the phrase means to bring sin upon oneself, not to bear sin on the offender's account.

Vengeance and the grudge are then distinguished by degree. Ellicott, with Gill, illustrates the first from the rabbis: a man refuses to lend his sickle, and the next day the same neighbour is told, I will not lend thee my hatchet, even as thou wouldest not lend me. The grudge goes further and is subtler, for the injured man is to banish the injury from memory although no reparation has been made. To lend the thing and say while lending it, I will not act as you acted, for you refused me, is already a breach of the command. Then comes the sentence that gathers the rest. Ellicott recalls Hillel, asked for the sum of the Law in the shortest possible time, who gave the precept negatively — what thou dost not wish others to do to thee, do not thou to others; this is the whole Law, the rest is its interpretation, now go and learn — where Christ gives it positively. Calvin turns it against the schools, which taught that a man must love himself first and his neighbour by that rule, the rule being superior to what it regulates. God did not set self-love up as the standard. It blinds us and is the parent of all iniquities, and the command cures it by transferring elsewhere the love already burning too fiercely within. Clarke removes a common mistake, that loving one's neighbour as oneself was first instituted under the gospel; what is new is only to love as Christ loved us. Wesley reads as thyself of sincerity rather than equality of affection.
19:
A new kind of law begins here, and Gill marks the change. What went before was moral, planted in the heart and agreeable to the light of nature; what follows is of positive institution and depends on the will of the lawgiver, which Jarchi calls the decree of a king who gives no reason for it. Keil and Delitzsch describe the series as making it a duty to keep the physical and moral order of the world sacred, beginning with a command not to mix what God separated in creating. Ellicott says the same from Genesis, where everything is made after its kind, so that to unite dissimilar things dissolves a divine distinction. Henry puts it as a rule of two halves: as what God has joined we must not separate, so what he has separated we must not join; we are to acquiesce in the order of nature and not covet monsters. Wesley gathers three purposes at once — to restrain men who would amend the works of God, to teach an abhorrence of unnatural lusts by a restraint laid even on the brutes, and to warn Israel off mixture with the nations in marriage and religion.

How far the prohibitions reach is worked out differently. Ellicott reports that the produce of such mixtures was never forbidden, so that the Jews used mules freely, bred without their help or imported; that the seed law was held to bind only in the Holy Land and only for food crops sown together, wheat with barley or beans with lentils, so that a fig tree in a vineyard breaks nothing; and that it was extended to grafting, an apple not to be grafted on a citron. On the garment he adds that a woollen coat might not even be mended with flaxen thread, one ancient reason given being that wool and linen were appointed for the priests alone. Clarke prefers plain husbandry where he can get it, since oats and wheat sown together leave the one injured and the other ruined, and the turnip and the carrot will not prosper in company. He confesses that nobody knows what the word for the mixed garment means, and suspects the law aimed at finery, illustrating it from a fourteenth-century sermon against the beau who wore hose of one colour on one leg and another on the other. Henry allows both readings, either a heathen custom forbidden or a warning against weaving the usages of the Gentiles into God's ordinances.

The bondmaid's case turns on what her betrothal was worth. Keil and Delitzsch see the personal rights of a slave upheld here, so that a maid was not degraded into mere property. Ellicott explains why the penalty falls short of death: her espousal was not legally complete, so she was not properly another man's wife; the scourging is hers alone, and only when she was proved a consenting party. The man's part follows separately, and he had to bring his ram whether he had sinned in ignorance or presumptuously, while she brought nothing, having as her master's property nothing of her own. Clarke supposes less self-command in a slave and so less guilt. Calvin will not let the leniency be misread. Before God there is no difference between bond and free, and the crime deserves death; the penalty is mitigated only in consideration of the people's infirmity. That the man already beaten with stripes still needed an expiation shows that the measure of an offence is not to be estimated by its punishment. Henry states the balance as the law's own: it was for the honour of marriage, though only begun by betrothing, that the crime should be punished at all, and for the honour of freedom that it should not be punished as the debauching of a free woman.
23:
The young fruit trees divide the commentators most sharply. Clarke sees no reason to look for mystical meanings, the fruit of a young tree being poor because its juices are not yet elaborated, and Ellicott agrees that the Lawgiver here enacts what careful husbandmen had always done, since early fruit is stunted and pinching it off makes the tree bear better afterwards, so that greedy owners are debarred from injuring themselves. Calvin reads it under the first commandment instead. The circumcision of trees was to let the Jews see a symbol of their own adoption in the very orchard, and to teach that whatever the earth produces is in a manner profane until purified, all things being sanctified by the word of God and prayer; not that anything is impure in itself, but that the earth has contracted pollution from the corruption of man. Wesley takes both at once, the rule serving the trees, which grow faster for being stripped early, and the men, who are taught to bridle their appetites. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the grammar, where the verb is formed from the noun and means to treat a thing as uncircumcised, that is, to throw it away as uneatable.

Ellicott notes that the metaphor is explained by the text itself, the same word being used of a stubborn heart and of lips and ears that will not do their work. He counts this among the four laws in Leviticus given prospectively, for a land the people had not yet entered, and reports how narrowly its scope was drawn afterwards. Trees the Canaanites had planted before Israel came were exempt, as were trees whose fruit was not human food, trees that grew up of themselves, and trees planted for hedges or timber. Where the law did apply it was pressed hard: no advantage of any kind might be taken of the first three years, the fruit being burnt or buried rather than sold, and a man who ate so much as an olive received forty stripes save one. Gill and Wesley follow the fourth year's produce to the priest, though Gill notes with Jarchi that it might be redeemed instead, as the tithe was that could not be eaten within the walls of Jerusalem, and Wesley adds that part went to the widow, the fatherless and the stranger. Ellicott has the owner carry it up himself and eat it in the holy city with the poor he invites, adding a fifth to the value if he redeems it. Both he and Calvin end where the law ends, on the promise attached: so far from losing by the three years' waiting, the man who keeps the rule is to look for the larger increase afterwards, which Wesley says only the blessing of God can give.
26:
What it means to eat with the blood is not agreed. Keil and Delitzsch read it as eating upon blood, that is, flesh not entirely cleansed of it, and take the verse for a strengthening rather than a repetition of the earlier law: not only was no blood to be eaten, but no flesh to which blood still adhered. Ellicott reports that the second Temple found five distinct prohibitions in the words, among them eating a slaughtered beast while the flesh still trembles, eating sacrificial flesh while the blood stands unsprinkled, and the meal eaten by a family on the day one of them is put to death. All five rest on the literal rendering, ye shall not eat by the blood. Others take that same rendering to point at an idolatrous practice, and Gill has it from Maimonides: the Zabians gathered the blood of their sacrifices into a vessel or a hole dug in the earth and sat round it to eat their meal beside it, reckoning that they thereby fraternised with the demons whose food they took blood to be. Calvin states the reason behind the whole group: God meant to sever his people from the heathen by setting an obstacle in the way, since there is nothing to which men are more prone than conforming to the customs of others, by which they communicate each other's vices.

The two words for the forbidden arts are obscure, and the commentators work at them from the roots. Keil and Delitzsch derive the first from a verb to whisper, or else from the noun for a serpent, so that it would mean divining by snakes and then divining by omens at large; and they deny that the second comes from the word for cloud, of which there is no historical trace in Hebrew, preferring the rabbinic derivation from the word for eye, to ogle and so to bewitch with an evil eye. Clarke keeps the cloud, and thinks the first may be what the Greeks called divination by serpents. Ellicott illustrates enchantment from the second Temple with a list of omens a man was forbidden to read: a morsel dropped from his mouth, a staff fallen from his hand, a crow cawing, a deer crossing his path, a serpent creeping on his right hand or a fox going by on his left. Observing times is to say that this is a good day to begin a journey and tomorrow will be lucky for a purchase. Wesley turns it forward. It was unpardonable in men to whom the oracles of God were committed to ask counsel of the devil, and worse in Christians, to whom the Son of God is manifested to destroy the devil's works, that they should have their nativities cast or their fortunes told.

The tonsure and the beard are traced to the same source. Keil and Delitzsch, with Gill and Ellicott, explain the rounding as cutting the hair in a circle from temple to temple, which Herodotus reports of certain Arab tribes in honour of their god Orotal. Clarke adds the Macians of Libya, who left a tuft on the crown as the Chinese do still, and shows what the hair was for. Parents dedicated their children's hair to a god, and the children cut it off and consecrated it when they came to manhood; so Achilles at the pyre of Patroclus cut off the golden locks his father had vowed to the river Sperchius and threw them into the flood, and in Virgil the topmost lock of Dido belonged to the powers below. Ellicott explains the beard by what it was worth. It was the greatest ornament of a man and as dear to him as life, and its mutilation the most degrading of punishments; and because it was so precious, some of the ancients offered the firstlings of it to their gods.
28:
Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as two prohibitions of one thing, the unnatural disfigurement of the body. The first belongs to the passionate outbursts of mourning common among the excitable nations of the East, and to the scratching of the arms, hands and face which is reported of the Babylonians and Armenians, the Scythians, and even the ancient Romans, and which is practised by Arabs, Persians and Abyssinians still; they note that it apparently held its ground among the Israelites in spite of the prohibition. Gill gathers the same customs in more detail. Jarchi calls it a usage of the Amorites; among the Scythians, for a dead king, they cut off part of the ear, shaved the hair round about, gashed the arms, wounded the forehead and nose, and drove arrows through the left hand; the Carthaginians tore their hair and their mouths and beat their breasts; and Roman women tore their cheeks until the law of the twelve tables had to forbid it. All of it, he says on Varro's authority, was to appease the infernal deities and give them satisfaction for the dead. Clarke reaches for Virgil, where the sister of Dido fouls her face with her nails and beats her breast with her fists. Wesley notes only that the Gentiles did this both in the worship of their idols and in their solemn mournings.

Ellicott states the reason the Israelite may not. He is created in the image of God and is to be holy as the Lord is holy, so he must not disfigure the body that carries that image, nor sorrow as others which have no hope; and for the breach of this law the offender took forty stripes save one. The printed marks he describes as punctures in the skin filled with ink or stibium, a practice found among savage and civilised nations alike: the slave bore the initials of his master, the soldier those of his general, and the worshipper the image of his tutelar deity. What the Law gives instead is the phylactery, a sign bound upon the hand and a memorial between the eyes, so that the emblem of a man's creed is worn without cutting it into him. Clarke says the same custom is still visible wherever men carry a mark in honour of what they worship, from the sectarian marks on the foreheads of the Hindoo castes to the crosses he has himself seen pricked into men's arms and rubbed with a blue colouring that is never afterwards effaced. He hears the practice behind the mark of the beast received in the hand and the forehead, and behind the word of Paul, who bore in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus.
29:
The prostituting of a daughter is placed by most of them in the idol temples. Gill points to the Canaanite practice Athanasius describes, where women prostituted themselves in the shrines of their idols; Ellicott names the worship of Astarte; Wesley says the Gentiles did it for the honour of idols to whom women were consecrated. Clarke supplies its commercial form: the Cyprian women, on Justin's authority, earned by public prostitution the portion their husbands received with them at marriage, and the Phoenicians made a gift to Venus of what they got by prostituting their daughters. Keil and Delitzsch will not have the verse turned into a figure. The whoredom meant is fleshly and not spiritual, since the word for the resulting vice is used in no other connection. Calvin widens the law rather than narrowing it. To read it of spiritual fornication is tame and forced, and those who confine it to public brothels restrict it too much, for what God requires is that parents preserve their daughters by a chaste education. Adultery is not in question here at all; the verse declares it criminal that a man and woman should have connection out of wedlock.

The sabbath and the sanctuary are then set together, and Keil and Delitzsch treat the pairing as a return to the chief point. Where the Lord's day is kept holy and reverence for his sanctuary lives in the heart, not only are many sins avoided, but domestic and social life is pervaded by the fear of God. Calvin ties the two tighter still. The service of the tabernacle was annexed to the sabbath by an indissoluble bond, the rest from labour having reference to the sacrifices, since it would be mere mockery to rest without an ulterior object. To fear the sanctuary is a figure for showing by reverence there how truly one fears the God who promised to be present in it. Ellicott gives the practical shape reverence took: a man was not to enter defiled, nor go up with his staff in his hand, his shoes on his feet, his working clothes on, or bags of money about him, nor to spit within the precincts nor make them a thoroughfare — and it is that last rule, he notes, that lies behind Christ's refusing to let any man carry a vessel through the Temple. Henry brings it forward: no place is now holy by institution as the tabernacle was, but the law still binds us to respect the assemblies of Christians, held under a promise of Christ's presence.

The last prohibition sends them all to the dictionary. Gill says the word for those with familiar spirits means bottles, whether because the diviner sat on something bottle-shaped, or divined by one, or swelled out like one when he answered; hence master or mistress of the bottle. He takes them for ventriloquists, and matches them with the Pythoness at Delphi and the maid in the Acts. Ellicott adds what the wizards did: they put in the mouth a bone of a bird called yaduâ and burned incense, and in the fumes fell into an ecstasy and foretold events. Keil and Delitzsch take the word for a departed spirit called up to disclose the future, the name passing afterwards to the necromancer himself. Clarke matches the inflation with Virgil's Sibyl, whose features enlarged and hair flew loose as the god came nearer, then presses the law past its letter. Not only real dealers with familiar spirits are forbidden but every pretender to the knowledge of the future, fortune-tellers and astrologers alike; for to seek what God has not thought proper to reveal is a sin against his wisdom and his goodness, who in great mercy hid the future from man and gave him hope in its place. Henry adds that this was the sin which completed the wickedness of Saul.
32:
Reverence for age is grounded on what God is. Keil and Delitzsch say plainly that God is honoured in the old man, and that this is why reverence for years is demanded; the virtue was cultivated by Egyptians, Spartans and old Romans alike. Ellicott reaches the same ground from the divine title itself, since he who requires the honour is called the Ancient of days; and he passes on two sayings of the second Temple, that a man who receives and cares for an old man is rewarded as though he had received God, and that prophets are believed only when they come armed with miracles, but old men always. He adds that orthodox Jews still rise when an aged person enters and will not sit until he bids them, workmen alone excepted. Gill fixes the ages, sixty for old age and seventy for grey hairs, and reports the tradition that a young man must rise while the elder is still four cubits off and sit again the moment he has passed, so that the rising is plainly for him. Wesley adds why the fear of God is annexed: the respect is due for God's sake if not for the man's, old age being his singular blessing.

Calvin makes the duty a matter of nature and not of statute only. Some sparks of God's majesty shine out in old men, by which they approach the honour owed to parents, and what is commanded here is dictated by nature itself. He proves it from a scene at Athens, where an old man came into the theatre and found no room among his own countrymen, but was received with honour by the Spartan ambassador, whereupon the applause of the whole house broke out and the Lacedaemonian cried that the Athenians knew what was right and would not do it. Calvin will not pretend the honour is always deserved. Many old men subvert their own dignity by levity or lewdness or sloth, and grey hairs are not always accompanied by wisdom; yet age in itself is venerable, because God has commanded that it be so.

The stranger closes the group, and Clarke calls the law humane and politic at once. None is so desolate as a stranger and none needs charity more, and the man unmoved by that desolation has neither benevolence nor charity; while as policy it drew people to settle rather than merely sojourn, so that the nation grew stronger. Ellicott describes who is meant: a man of foreign birth who had joined the faith, circumcised, fasting on the Day of Atonement, bound by the laws of sacrifice and chastity like a native. Not vexing him, he says, forbids upbraiding him with his nationality or throwing his old idolatry at him, and forbids the words foreigner and neophyte, which every civilised nation and religious community is still prone to use. Gill would extend the term further, to a proselyte of the gate or to any stranger providentially cast among them, and Keil and Delitzsch note that the law goes past forbearance to love. Calvin explains why the case had to be named at all. Had strangers gone unmentioned, Israel would have thought that injuring no one of their own nation discharged the whole duty; naming them teaches that equity is to be cultivated constantly and towards all men. God interposes here because such men have nobody to take their part, as with the widow and the orphan; and the name of neighbour is not confined to our kindred but reaches the whole human race, as Christ showed in the Samaritan. Ellicott and Wesley both end where the verse ends, on Egypt: Israel knew from the inside what it was to be used inhumanly for being strangers. Ellicott adds that this one law drew so many into the land that Solomon could count a hundred and fifty thousand of them.
35:
Ellicott notices that the words used of the balance are those used earlier of the bench. A man who declares a false measure legal is therefore as much a corrupt judge as one who knowingly passes a wrong sentence in court. Because men who would scorn plain theft grow lax about weights, Scripture brands such dealing an abomination. He reports the five charges the second Temple laid against the false measurer, the same five it laid against the corrupt judge: he defiles the land, profanes the name of God, drives away the Shechinah, and makes Israel fall by the sword and go into captivity. Hence their saying that the sin of illegal weights is greater than incest, and equal to denying that God redeemed Israel out of Egypt. They set public overseers to inspect weights throughout the country. Gill and Ellicott both report the rule about the material: weights were not to be made of iron or lead or any metal that would grow lighter with rust or wear, but of polished rock or glass. Gill adds from Jarchi why the two subjects belong together: a measurer is himself a judge, and perverts judgment when he deals deceitfully.

Calvin allows the narrower reading and then passes it. If judgment is taken strictly, the verse is a special charge to judges; but the word often means rectitude, so that all iniquity contrary to integrity is condemned here. His reason for treating false measure as one of the gravest is social rather than commercial. If the laws of buying and selling are corrupted, human society is in a manner dissolved, so that the man who cheats with a false weight differs little from the man who utters false coin — and Roman law agreed, condemning such a one to double the amount, with banishment to an island by a decree of Hadrian. He notes that even where no legal punishment follows, God summons the conscience to his own tribunal by a promise and a threat. The connection of long life with a just weight is only figurative; but since the avaricious are too devoted to this transitory life, God holds out to them the very thing they overvalue, to draw them off from blind and impetuous covetousness. And the closing words settle the scope: after saying he abhors all who do such things, he explains himself by adding, all that do unrighteously.

Clarke divides the field into four, which between them take in everything that can pass between a man and his fellow: judgment, where the magistrate decides by the law; the mete-yard, for length and surface; weight, for whatever is weighed against the standards kept in the sanctuary; and measure, for capacity, the homer and ephah and seah and hin and omer and kab and log. He notes with Gill that the word rendered weights is simply stones, which is why men still reckon by the stone. Ellicott sizes the two named measures, the ephah of ten omers for dry goods, answering to the bath for liquids, and the hin, which held as much as seventy-two hens' eggs; both stand for all the rest, as Wesley says too. Keil and Delitzsch add what Deuteronomy forbids in renewing the law, the carrying of stone and stone in the bag, a large weight and a small, or the keeping of two measures, a full one to buy with and a scant one to sell by. Calvin reads the closing formula as the preface to the whole law repeated: God argues partly from his authority, since the Creator of heaven and earth may justly claim supreme dominion, and partly from the blessing of redemption, that men may submit willingly to one from whom they have their safety. Wesley puts the same thing in a sentence, that God's deliverances are not indulgences to sin but greater obligations to every duty towards God and men.
